_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for Haiti covering Taíno cacicazgos (Hispaniola), Columbus 1492, Spanish colonization, French Saint-Domingue (richest colony in world), sugar/slavery (half million enslaved, Code Noir, brutal conditions), Haitian Revolution 1791-1804 (only successful slave revolution, Toussaint Louverture, Dessalines, defeated Napoleon), first Black republic, independence 1804, France's extortionate indemnity (150M francs, economic crippling), Duvalier dictatorships (Papa Doc/Baby Doc), political instability, 2010 earthquake (300,000 dead), and ongoing crises.

country_profile.government_type: Unitary semi-presidential republic (effectively failed state since 2021 assassination)

religion.note: Vodou officially recognized 2003 (widely practiced alongside Christianity, most Haitians practice both); West African Fon/Yoruba roots; lwa spirits; houngan/mambo priests; syncretic with Catholicism; demonized by outsiders; Papa Doc exploited Vodou imagery (Tonton Macoutes); evangelical growth

ethnic_groups.name: Black/African descent
ethnic_groups.notes: Descendants of enslaved West Africans (Fon, Yoruba, Kongo); revolutionary heritage (only successful slave revolt in history); Haitian Creole culture; Taíno completely exterminated by Spanish

ethnic_groups.name: Mulatto (Mixed)
ethnic_groups.notes: African-French mixed; historically formed elite ('mulatto elite'); afranchi (free coloreds) pre-revolution; controlled commerce/land; color-class tension central to Haitian history (light-skinned elite vs dark-skinned majority); gens de couleur

ethnic_groups.name: Other
ethnic_groups.notes: Syrian/Lebanese ('Syriens', commercial class); small white/European; Arab descent significant in commerce

independence.from: France (only successful slave revolution in history)

country_profile.notes_unique: First independent Black republic (1804); only country founded by a slave revolt; Haitian Revolution (1791-1804, defeated Napoleon's army, inspired abolition worldwide); France demanded 150M franc indemnity 1825 (paid until 1947, ~$21B in today's money, crippled economy); Citadelle Laferrière (UNESCO, largest fortress in Americas); Vodou; Duvalier dynasty (Papa Doc 1957-71, Baby Doc 1971-86, Tonton Macoutes death squads, estimated 30,000-60,000 killed); 2010 earthquake (~300,000 dead, Port-au-Prince devastated); President Moïse assassinated July 2021; gang control of Port-au-Prince 2023-present (80% territory); poorest country in Western Hemisphere; deforestation (2% forest remaining vs DR's 28%); diaspora (Miami/Montreal/NYC)

comparative_rankings._note: Country position relative to continent and global. 'rank' = 1 is best/largest.

current_government.name: Transitional Presidential Council
current_government.title: Collective leadership (no elected president)
current_government.notes: After PM Ariel Henry ousted; 7-member council; gangs control 80% of Port-au-Prince; Kenya-led multinational security force (MSS); no elections since 2016; effectively failed state

former_leaders.name: Ariel Henry
former_leaders.notes: PM (de facto head, no president); appointed by Moïse before assassination; never elected; forced out while abroad; gang uprising (Jimmy 'Barbecue' Chérizier)

former_leaders.name: Jovenel Moïse
former_leaders.notes: PHTK; banana exporter; assassinated July 7, 2021 at home by Colombian/American mercenaries (still unsolved conspiracy); ruled by decree (no parliament); controversial

former_leaders.name: Michel Martelly ('Sweet Micky')
former_leaders.notes: PHTK; kompa musician; populist; no elections held; corruption; USAID/Clinton Foundation post-earthquake controversies

former_leaders.name: René Préval
former_leaders.notes: Lavalas (initially); agronomist; only president to serve two terms and leave peacefully; 2010 earthquake response; moderate

former_leaders.name: Jean-Bertrand Aristide
former_leaders.notes: Liberation theology priest; first democratically elected president; overthrown twice (1991 military coup, 2004 US/France-backed); Lavalas movement; populist; controversial; lives in Haiti

former_leaders.name: Jean-Claude 'Baby Doc' Duvalier
former_leaders.notes: Succeeded father at age 19; playboy; continued repression; Tonton Macoutes; fled to France 1986 (overthrown by popular uprising); returned 2011; died 2014

former_leaders.name: François 'Papa Doc' Duvalier
former_leaders.notes: Country doctor turned dictator; President for Life 1964; Tonton Macoutes paramilitary; Vodou imagery for control; estimated 30,000-60,000 killed; anti-mulatto; Cold War US tolerance; died in office

former_leaders.name: Jean-Jacques Dessalines
former_leaders.notes: Independence hero; declared independence Jan 1, 1804; Emperor Jacques I; ordered massacre of remaining French; assassinated 1806; national hero

910.name: Taíno and Indigenous Peoples of Ayiti
910.description: The pre-Columbian indigenous civilizations of Hispaniola, from early Archaic Age migrations through the flourishing Taíno chiefdoms that named the island Ayiti ('land of high mountains') and developed complex agricultural societies.

sub_clusters.name: Archaic Age Migrations and Early Settlement
sub_clusters.description: The earliest inhabitants, the Ciboney and other Archaic Age peoples, who migrated from Central and South America to Hispaniola and established hunter-gatherer communities across the island.

sub_clusters.name: Taíno Chiefdoms and Cacicazgos
sub_clusters.description: The Taíno people, part of the Arawak language family, migrated from the Orinoco delta and established sophisticated agricultural societies with complex political structures organized into cacicazgos (chiefdoms) governed by caciques.

sub_clusters.name: Peak of Taíno Civilization
sub_clusters.description: At the time of European contact, Hispaniola was divided into five major Taíno cacicazgos — Marién, Maguá, Maguana, Jaragua, and Higüey — with an estimated population of several hundred thousand to over one million people practicing advanced agriculture, ball games, and elaborate religious ceremonies.
key_events: Five great cacicazgos govern Hispaniola by the 15th century
Taíno develop complex agriculture including conuco mound cultivation

920.name: Columbus, Spanish Conquest, and the Destruction of the Taíno
920.description: Christopher Columbus's arrival at Hispaniola in 1492, the founding of La Navidad and La Isabela, the rapid enslavement and decimation of the Taíno population through forced labor and European diseases, and the establishment of Santo Domingo as Spain's first permanent New World capital.

sub_clusters.name: Columbus's Arrival and First Contact
sub_clusters.description: Columbus landed on the northern coast of Hispaniola on December 5, 1492, established the short-lived fort La Navidad from the wreck of the Santa María, and on his second voyage founded La Isabela in 1494. Santo Domingo, founded in 1496, became the first permanent European settlement in the Americas.
key_events: Columbus arrives at Hispaniola on December 5, 1492
Founding of Santo Domingo in 1496 — first permanent European city in the Americas

sub_clusters.name: Taíno Genocide and the Encomienda System
sub_clusters.description: The Spanish imposed the encomienda and repartimiento systems of forced labor, combined with European diseases (smallpox, measles, typhus), causing catastrophic demographic collapse. The Taíno population fell from hundreds of thousands to near extinction within fifty years.

sub_clusters.name: Early Spanish Colony and Western Decline
sub_clusters.description: As Spain shifted focus to gold-rich Mexico and Peru, western Hispaniola was depopulated and neglected, creating a power vacuum that attracted buccaneers and French settlers to the island's western shores.

930.name: French Saint-Domingue: The Pearl of the Antilles
930.description: The rise of French colonial Saint-Domingue from buccaneer haven to the wealthiest colony in the Caribbean, powered by a brutal sugar plantation system that imported hundreds of thousands of enslaved Africans and generated immense wealth for France.

sub_clusters.name: Buccaneers and French Settlement
sub_clusters.description: French buccaneers and filibusters established settlements on Tortuga (Île de la Tortue) and the western coast of Hispaniola. France formally gained sovereignty over the western third of the island through the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697, creating the colony of Saint-Domingue.
key_events: French buccaneers settle Tortuga in the 1620s–1630s
Treaty of Ryswick 1697 cedes western Hispaniola to France

sub_clusters.name: Sugar Revolution and the Plantation System
sub_clusters.description: Saint-Domingue was transformed into a vast sugar, coffee, and indigo production zone. By the mid-18th century, it produced roughly 40% of Europe's sugar and 60% of its coffee, making it the richest colony in the world and earning the name 'Pearl of the Antilles.'

sub_clusters.name: Enslaved Population, Vodou, and Resistance
sub_clusters.description: By the 1780s, nearly 500,000 enslaved Africans labored under extraordinarily brutal conditions; the average life expectancy after arrival was seven years. Enslaved people preserved African spiritual practices that evolved into Vodou, and maroon communities maintained armed resistance in the mountains.
key_events: François Mackandal leads maroon resistance and alleged poisoning campaign, executed 1758
Saint-Domingue enslaved population reaches approximately 500,000 by 1789

sub_clusters.name: Gens de Couleur Libres and Colonial Social Hierarchy
sub_clusters.description: The complex three-tiered racial hierarchy of Saint-Domingue: grands blancs (wealthy white planters), petits blancs (poor whites), and gens de couleur libres (free people of color, many wealthy and slave-owning themselves). Increasing racial legislation restricted free coloreds despite their economic power.

930.name: The Haitian Revolution
930.description: The only successful large-scale slave revolution in history, a thirteen-year struggle that destroyed the wealthiest colony in the Caribbean, defeated the armies of France, Spain, and Britain, and produced the first independent Black republic and the second independent nation in the Western Hemisphere.

sub_clusters.name: French Revolution Spillover and Early Uprisings
sub_clusters.description: The French Revolution's ideals of liberty and equality destabilized Saint-Domingue's racial hierarchy. Vincent Ogé led a failed mulatto uprising in 1790 demanding rights for free people of color.
key_events: Vincent Ogé's rebellion for free colored rights, 1790 — executed 1791

sub_clusters.name: The Great Slave Insurrection of 1791
sub_clusters.description: On the night of August 22, 1791, enslaved people in the northern plain launched a massive coordinated insurrection, traditionally preceded by the Vodou ceremony at Bois Caïman led by the houngan Dutty Boukman. Within weeks, over 1,000 plantations were destroyed.
key_events: Bois Caïman Vodou ceremony — August 14, 1791
Great slave insurrection begins August 22, 1791

sub_clusters.name: Toussaint Louverture and the Struggle for Control
sub_clusters.description: Toussaint Louverture emerged as the revolutionary leader, skillfully playing France, Spain, and Britain against each other. He defeated British and Spanish forces, reunified the entire island, and promulgated a constitution in 1801 making himself Governor-General for life.
key_events: Toussaint defeats British invasion force 1798
Toussaint promulgates autonomous constitution 1801
Napoleon sends Leclerc expedition; Toussaint captured and sent to France 1802

sub_clusters.name: Dessalines and the Declaration of Independence
sub_clusters.description: After Toussaint's capture, Jean-Jacques Dessalines and Henri Christophe continued the war. Napoleon's attempt to restore slavery galvanized resistance. The French army was devastated by yellow fever and military defeats. Dessalines declared independence on January 1, 1804, restoring the Taíno name 'Haiti.'
key_events: Battle of Vertières — decisive defeat of French forces, November 18, 1803
Declaration of Haitian independence — January 1, 1804

940.name: The Early Republic and 19th-Century Struggles
940.description: Haiti's turbulent first century as an independent nation: internal divisions between north and south, the crushing French indemnity debt, international isolation, repeated political instability, and the reunification and subsequent re-separation from Santo Domingo.

sub_clusters.name: Dessalines, Christophe, and Pétion: A Nation Divided
sub_clusters.description: Dessalines was assassinated in 1806, and Haiti split into Henri Christophe's northern Kingdom (who built the Citadelle Laferrière) and Alexandre Pétion's southern Republic. Pétion aided Simón Bolívar's liberation struggles in exchange for abolishing slavery.
key_events: Assassination of Emperor Dessalines 1806
Henri Christophe builds the Citadelle Laferrière, completed c. 1820
Pétion provides refuge and aid to Simón Bolívar 1816

sub_clusters.name: Boyer, Island Reunification, and the French Indemnity
sub_clusters.description: Jean-Pierre Boyer reunified Haiti in 1820 and conquered Spanish Santo Domingo in 1822. In 1825, France imposed a crushing 150-million-franc indemnity (later reduced to 90 million) as the price of diplomatic recognition — a debt that crippled Haiti's development for over a century.
key_events: Boyer conquers Santo Domingo 1822 — unifies the island
France demands 150-million-franc indemnity for recognition 1825

sub_clusters.name: Political Instability and International Isolation
sub_clusters.description: After Boyer's overthrow in 1843, Haiti experienced chronic political instability with frequent coups and short-lived presidencies. The United States did not recognize Haiti until 1862. The country remained diplomatically isolated as Western powers refused to acknowledge a Black republic.

950.name: United States Occupation of Haiti
950.description: The period of escalating political chaos, culminating in the U.S. Marines' invasion and nineteen-year occupation (1915–1934), which brought infrastructure improvements but also racial brutality, corvée forced labor, and Haitian resistance including the Cacos guerrilla wars.

sub_clusters.name: Pre-Occupation Political Crisis
sub_clusters.description: Between 1911 and 1915, Haiti had six presidents in rapid succession — several killed or overthrown. President Vilbrun Guillaume Sam was lynched by a mob in July 1915, providing the pretext for U.S. intervention.

sub_clusters.name: U.S. Marine Occupation 1915–1934
sub_clusters.description: U.S. Marines occupied Haiti from July 1915 to August 1934. The occupation imposed a new constitution (partly authored by Franklin D. Roosevelt), reintroduced corvée forced labor, and provoked the Caco guerrilla resistance led by Charlemagne Péralte, who was killed in 1919.
key_events: U.S. Marines invade Haiti — July 28, 1915
Charlemagne Péralte leads Caco resistance — killed November 1, 1919
U.S. occupation ends August 1934

950.name: The Duvalier Dynasty: Papa Doc and Baby Doc
950.description: Post-occupation Haiti's struggle for stability, the rise of François 'Papa Doc' Duvalier and his Tonton Macoutes terror apparatus, followed by his son Jean-Claude 'Baby Doc' Duvalier's continuation of authoritarian rule until the popular uprising of 1986.

sub_clusters.name: Post-Occupation Instability and Estimé Era
sub_clusters.description: After the U.S. withdrawal, Haiti experienced continued political turmoil. Dumarsais Estimé (1946–1950) promoted Black nationalism and social reforms before being overthrown by Paul Magloire, whose own corruption led to his ouster.

sub_clusters.name: François 'Papa Doc' Duvalier's Dictatorship
sub_clusters.description: François Duvalier won the 1957 election on a Black nationalist platform, then consolidated totalitarian power through the paramilitary Tonton Macoutes (Volontaires de la Sécurité Nationale). He declared himself President for Life in 1964 and ruled through terror, political murders, and Vodou mysticism until his death.
key_events: Duvalier elected president 1957
Duvalier declares himself President for Life 1964
Death of Papa Doc — April 21, 1971; succeeded by 19-year-old son

sub_clusters.name: Jean-Claude 'Baby Doc' Duvalier and Popular Uprising
sub_clusters.description: Jean-Claude Duvalier inherited power at age 19, initially pursuing limited liberalization before reverting to repression and kleptocracy. A popular uprising fueled by poverty, the ti legliz (liberation theology) movement, and international pressure forced Baby Doc into exile on February 7, 1986.
key_events: Baby Doc flees Haiti — February 7, 1986

950.name: Democratic Transition and Aristide Era
950.description: Haiti's turbulent transition from dictatorship to democracy, including the 1987 constitution, the election and repeated overthrows of Jean-Bertrand Aristide, military junta rule, and the 1994 U.S.-led intervention to restore democratic governance.

sub_clusters.name: Post-Duvalier Transition and 1987 Constitution
sub_clusters.description: The fall of Baby Doc was followed by a period of military-civilian government, a new democratic constitution ratified in 1987, and the Ruelle Vaillant massacre of voters at polling stations that derailed the first election attempt.

sub_clusters.name: Aristide, Military Coups, and International Intervention
sub_clusters.description: Jean-Bertrand Aristide, a liberation theology priest, won a landslide election in 1990 but was overthrown by a military coup in September 1991. A brutal military junta under Raoul Cédras ruled until a U.S.-led intervention restored Aristide in October 1994.
key_events: Aristide wins first free election — December 1990
Military coup overthrows Aristide — September 30, 1991
U.S.-led Operation Uphold Democracy restores Aristide — October 1994

960.name: 21st-Century Crises and Resilience
960.description: Contemporary Haiti's compounding catastrophes: the second Aristide ouster, the devastating 2010 earthquake, the cholera epidemic, Hurricane Matthew, political dysfunction, the assassination of President Moïse, and the ongoing gang crisis — alongside remarkable Haitian cultural resilience and diaspora engagement.

sub_clusters.name: Aristide's Second Fall and MINUSTAH
sub_clusters.description: Aristide was re-elected in 2000 amid controversy and ousted again in February 2004 amid armed rebellion. The UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti (MINUSTAH) deployed to maintain order but was itself plagued by scandals.

sub_clusters.name: The 2010 Earthquake and Its Aftermath
sub_clusters.description: On January 12, 2010, a magnitude 7.0 earthquake struck near Port-au-Prince, killing an estimated 220,000–316,000 people, displacing 1.5 million, and destroying much of the capital's infrastructure. The massive international aid response was marred by dysfunction and the MINUSTAH-introduced cholera epidemic that killed over 10,000.
key_events: Magnitude 7.0 earthquake devastates Port-au-Prince — January 12, 2010
UN-introduced cholera epidemic begins October 2010 — kills over 10,000

sub_clusters.name: Political Instability, Moïse Assassination, and Gang Crisis
sub_clusters.description: Haiti descended into deepening political crisis under President Jovenel Moïse, who was assassinated on July 7, 2021. Armed gangs — many with political connections — seized control of vast areas of Port-au-Prince, creating a humanitarian catastrophe and near-state collapse. A Kenyan-led multinational security support mission deployed in 2024.
key_events: President Jovenel Moïse assassinated — July 7, 2021
Gang coalitions seize control of Port-au-Prince 2023–2024
Kenya-led Multinational Security Support mission deploys 2024

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
